drapeaux.note: The French places Esther Hoffe's death in 2007 and the Supreme Court ruling in 2016 (nine years apart) but says the trial that followed lasted seven years; this may be consistent if the proceedings began in 2009, but it is not stated. Rendered as in the French, not corrected.

titre: The Will That Max Brod Did Not Honor
accroche: In 1924, Franz Kafka asks his friend to burn everything after his death. Max Brod refuses, and publishes it all, without having the right to.
contenu_vulgarise:
Franz Kafka dies on June 3, 1924, at forty, of a tuberculosis that prevents him from eating. He leaves his friend Max Brod written instructions, unambiguous: everything he has written and not published, manuscripts, diaries, letters, is to be burned, unread. Brod does not comply. Better still: he had already warned Kafka, during his lifetime, that he would categorically refuse to obey such a request.

## A Disobedience That Makes a Writer

Brod does not merely keep the papers, he publishes them. *Le Procès* (*The Trial*) appears in 1925, *Le Château* (*The Castle*) in 1926, *Amerika* in 1927. The writer the world knows today, the three unfinished novels, the stories, the *Journal* (*Diaries*), exists only because his executor did exactly the opposite of what he was asked. Kafka, in his lifetime, had published only a few stories in obscure journals.

The manuscripts themselves then go through a turbulent century. When the German army invades Prague, on March 19, 1939, Brod flees the same day for Palestine with a suitcase containing Kafka's papers. Part of the collection passes, in 1956, into a bank vault in Zurich, until the region stabilizes; in 1961, the academic Malcolm Pasley withdraws it and deposits it at the Bodleian Library in Oxford, where it now makes up most of the Kafka archives held outside Israel.

## A Second Will, a Second Disobedience

The story could end there. Yet it rebounds, identically, a generation later. On his death in 1968, Brod bequeaths to his secretary Esther Hoffe the papers still in his possession, with an equally clear instruction: to entrust them to a public institution in Israel. Hoffe does not do so. She keeps them, then, at her death in 2007, passes them to her two daughters, who inherit a dispute more than a treasure. The trial that follows lasts seven years. On August 8, 2016, the Supreme Court of Israel rules: the manuscripts go to the National Library of Israel, ninety-two years after Kafka's death.

## What It Shifts

The mechanism repeats itself point for point: an author states a precise last wish, his executor judges it unworthy of being followed, a court must decide decades later what a single person could have settled in his lifetime. Literary posterity sometimes hangs by a thread, the conscience of a friend who decides, alone, that the work deserves to outlive its author.

repere.texte: On August 8, 2016, the Supreme Court of Israel awards all of Kafka's manuscripts held by Max Brod's heirs to the National Library of Israel, ninety-two years after the writer's death.

carte.punch: Kafka asked for everything to be burned. His friend disobeyed, and published The Trial and The Castle.
carte.idee: In 1924, Franz Kafka asks Max Brod to burn all his unpublished manuscripts. Brod refuses and publishes them. Passed from Oxford to Israel over the course of the century, these same papers were still the subject of a trial in 2016: Brod's legatee, in turn, had not honored his last wishes.

quiz.question: Why were Kafka's manuscripts the subject of a new trial in 2016, ninety-two years after his death?
choix: Because a German court demanded their return as property looted during the war
Because Max Brod's legatee had kept the documents for her daughters, instead of entrusting them to a public institution as he had asked
Because the University of Oxford and the National Library of Israel were disputing the collection deposited in 1961
Because Kafka's own heirs were claiming royalties on the works published by Brod
quiz.explication: The 2016 dispute concerns not Kafka but Brod: his will of 1968 asked that the manuscripts go to a public institution in Israel. His legatee, Esther Hoffe, kept them and then passed them to her daughters. Not a wartime claim, nor a rivalry between libraries, nor a claim by Kafka's heirs: a second testamentary disobedience, half a century after the first.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did Franz Kafka publish in his lifetime?
choix: His entire body of work, before withdrawing it from sale
Only a few stories, in obscure journals
Nothing at all, no text bore his name before 1925
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In his lifetime, Kafka published only a few stories in obscure journals; his three novels appeared only after his death, thanks to Max Brod's disobedience.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How do Kafka's manuscripts escape the German invasion of Prague in 1939?
choix: They are hidden in the walls of Kafka's apartment until the end of the war
Max Brod takes them in a suitcase, fleeing to Palestine on the very day of the invasion
They are entrusted to the British embassy before being shipped to Oxford
A Czechoslovak postal worker smuggles them into Switzerland
quiz_supplementaire.explication: On March 19, 1939, the day of the German invasion, Brod flees Prague for Palestine with a suitcase containing Kafka's papers, which would pass through a vault in Zurich only in 1956.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where are Kafka's manuscripts kept between 1956 and 1961, before joining the Bodleian Library in Oxford?
choix: In a bank vault in Zurich
In the archives of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem
At the home of Max Brod's secretary, Esther Hoffe
In a Red Cross warehouse in Geneva
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Part of the collection passes, from 1956, through a bank vault in Zurich, before the academic Malcolm Pasley deposits it at the Bodleian Library in Oxford in 1961.
